assumptions: The incident is recorded as ending when it was escalated to humans, not when service recovered. There is no evidence in the data that the error rate returned to baseline; the last logs read still show the failing errors at their highest observed level. Customer impact should be assumed to have continued past the recorded end time until a human intervened.

The attempted mitigation (reverting the feature flag) is assumed not to have taken effect: the flag-evaluation log lines continue to report the feature as fully 'on' for every minute after the revert was issued. Why the revert did not land - a provider write that failed silently, client-side flag caching in the service, a competing write, or a revert applied to the wrong target (the action was recorded against a null target) - was not determined and needs to be checked against the flag provider's audit log.

The defective code is assumed to have been shipped in some earlier release that predates the change windows queried; no deployment record was found to confirm this. The conclusion that this was a flag exposure rather than a bad deploy rests on the absence of change events, which is weaker evidence than a positive identification of the commit.

Impact is assumed to be confined to the account page, because that is the only request type appearing in the error logs. Whether the same flag-gated code is reachable from other surfaces was not checked.
Traffic is assumed to be steady through the window (the logs report a constant 200 flag evaluations per minute), so the per-minute error percentages are treated as comparable to one another.

The low-confidence theory that the flag was re-enabled by the automation one second before the 'off' action was recorded was never tested and is not supported by anything beyond the ordering of two log entries.
input.executive_summary:
Shortly after midnight UTC on 14 September, a change was made to switch on a new billing-related feature for the online shop. The new feature contained a defect that caused the customer account page to fail outright whenever the feature was active for a request. The feature was switched on gradually over about a minute and then to all traffic, and account page failures rose immediately and stayed elevated. Customers trying to view their account page during this window saw errors; other parts of the shop were not implicated by the evidence gathered.

Monitoring detected the elevated failures about five minutes after they began, and automated triage identified the feature switch as the cause within a minute. An automated attempt to turn the feature back off was issued roughly one minute later, but the service did not recover: the shop's own logs continued to report the feature as switched on, and account page failures continued at the same level until the incident was handed to humans a few minutes later. At the point of escalation the problem had not been resolved and the impact was still ongoing. The permanent fix is to confirm the feature is genuinely disabled for all traffic and then correct the defect in the feature's code before re-enabling it.
input.root_cause: Enabling the `monthly-spend-feature` flag on io-shop exposed a code path on the account page that raises `ZeroDivisionError`, so every request that evaluated the flag as "on" failed. The rollout began at 00:01Z as a partial ramp (137 off / 63 on in that minute) and went fully on from 00:02Z; the per-minute error rate tracked the ramp exactly, and the pre-onset `UpstreamTimeout` errors were displaced by `ZeroDivisionError` at the same moment. No deploy or release appears anywhere in the change history queried (6-hour, 12-hour and ~4-day lookbacks), so the flag toggle — not a code push — is the proximate trigger; the defective code itself was presumably already latent in production behind the flag.
